newsitem.title: USA: Shell, Chevron at odds on status of Turk pipeline.
newsitem.headline: Shell, Chevron at odds on status of Turk pipeline.

text.p: Shell and Chevron gave conflicting statements Thursday regarding reports that a joint venture to build a pipeline from the Azeri capital of Baku to the Turkish port of Ceyhan had been completed.
"There's no formal deal," said Mike Libbey, spokesman for Chevron.
Turkish energy minister Recai Kutan said earlier that Turkey agreed to set up the pipeline with Shell, Italy's Eni, Chevron and Unocal.

"For a long time we've had an interest in oil and gas in the former Soviet Union and as an operator of the Tengiz field. We are also interested in any potential commercial project that would help bring oil from Tengiz Field and that region to world markets," Libbey said. "We are not familiar with the specifics of the joint venture referred to."
However, Shell confirmed that the pipeline deal was underway.

"We've got an agreement from the Turkish authorities to negotiate for an oil pipeline. We're working on a joint venture agreement and hope to conclude a deal shortly," a Shell spokesman said. He would not comment on Chevron's statements.

Chevron did participate in a World Bank meeting in Ankara on May 2, though no formal agreement was reached, Libbey said, and the meeting was only preliminary. Shell oil officials did not attend that meeting, he added.
The Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) will build a 990 mile (1,580 km) pipeline from the Kazakhstan's Tengiz oil field to to Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossisk.
Chevron, which holds the largest stake in the CPC at 15 percent, has also developed a $20 billion venture with Mobil in Tengiz.
